Apple's FY2025 10-K (Item 1A, Risk Factors) discloses three primary supply chain risk factors: dependence on outsourced manufacturing and logistics partners concentrated in Asia, reliance on single/limited-source and custom components, and exposure to trade restrictions, tariffs and geopolitical tensions.

- **Dependence on outsourcing partners (p.10):** A significant majority of Apple's manufacturing is performed by outsourcing partners located primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam, with single-source partners in the U.S., Asia and Europe supplying many components and partners primarily in Asia performing final assembly of substantially all hardware products. Apple has also outsourced much of its transportation and logistics management. These arrangements lower operating costs but reduce direct control over production and distribution, which has from time to time adversely affected cost, quality or quantity; Apple generally remains responsible to consumers for warranty service on product defects, and supplier code of conduct violations occur from time to time. Changes or additions to the supply chain require considerable time and resources and carry additional regulatory and operational risks.

- **Obtaining components in sufficient quantities on commercially reasonable terms (pp.10–11):** Certain components come from single or limited sources, exposing Apple to significant supply and pricing risks, and even multi-source components are subject to industry-wide shortages and commodity price fluctuations — the filing cites past global semiconductor shortages as an example. New products often use custom components available from only one source, with initial capacity constraints until supplier yields mature; Apple may not be able to extend or renew supply agreements, and suppliers may fail, consolidate, or prioritize common components over Apple's custom ones.

- **Trade restrictions, tariffs and geopolitical tensions (p.8):** Restrictions on international trade — tariffs and import/export controls on goods, technology or data — can materially adversely affect Apple's business and supply chain, increasing costs or limiting availability of products, components, and rare earths and other raw materials, and potentially forcing supplier changes and operational restructuring. The filing specifically flags the new U.S. tariffs announced beginning in the second quarter of 2025 on imports from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and the EU, threatened reciprocal tariffs, and a Section 232 investigation into semiconductor imports. It also notes global supply chains are highly concentrated and that escalation of geopolitical tensions or conflict could result in significant disruptions.

- Related disclosures reinforce these risks: business interruptions from political events, natural disasters, public health issues and industrial accidents can affect suppliers, contract manufacturers and logistics providers (p.8), and supply shortages and higher component and outside manufacturing costs are cited as sources of net sales and gross margin pressure (p.17).

Sources: [AAPL FY2025 10-K, p.8], [AAPL FY2025 10-K, p.10], [AAPL FY2025 10-K, p.11], [AAPL FY2025 10-K, p.17]

Apple's FY2025 10-K discloses two dedicated supply chain risk factors in Item 1A — dependence on outsourced manufacturing/logistics partners and obtaining components in sufficient quantities — plus related trade-restriction and business-interruption risks.

**1. Dependence on outsourcing partners for manufacturing and logistics (p.10)**
- Most manufacturing is done by outsourcing partners, primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam, plus U.S. sourcing; single-source partners in the U.S., Asia and Europe supply many components, partners primarily in Asia do final assembly of substantially all hardware, and much of transportation/logistics management is outsourced.
- These arrangements lower operating costs but reduce direct control over production and distribution, which has at times adversely affected cost, quality or quantity of products and flexibility to respond to changing conditions.
- Apple remains responsible to consumers for warranty and out-of-warranty service despite defect-reimbursement provisions, and experiences unanticipated product defect liabilities; supplier code of conduct violations occur from time to time and can materially adversely affect the business.
- Supply chain changes or additions require considerable time and resources and carry significant risks, including additional regulatory and operational risks.

**2. Obtaining components in sufficient quantities on commercially reasonable terms (pp.10–11)**
- Certain components come from single or limited sources, creating significant supply and pricing risks; even multi-source components face industry-wide shortages and commodity price fluctuations — past global semiconductor shortages are cited as an example that could recur.
- New products often use custom components from only one source, with initial capacity constraints until supplier yields mature; Apple may not extend or renew supply agreements on similar terms, or at all, or find alternatives.
- Suppliers may fail, consolidate, or shift to common components instead of Apple-customized ones, exposing Apple to shortages and price increases.

**Related supply chain risks elsewhere in Item 1A**
- Trade restrictions and tariffs (p.8): new U.S. tariffs announced beginning Q2 2025 on imports from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and the EU, with reciprocal/retaliatory measures threatened and a Section 232 semiconductor import investigation underway; these can raise costs or limit availability of products, components, rare earths and other raw materials, and may force supplier changes and operational restructuring. Global supply chains are highly concentrated; escalating geopolitical tensions or conflict could cause significant disruptions.
- Business interruptions (p.8): political events, trade disputes, geopolitical tensions, conflict, terrorism, natural disasters, public health issues and industrial accidents can materially adversely affect suppliers, contract manufacturers and logistics providers.
- Margin pressure (p.17): supply shortages and potential increases in component and outside manufacturing costs are listed among factors pressuring net sales and gross margins.

Sources: [AAPL FY2025 10-K, p.10], [AAPL FY2025 10-K, p.11], [AAPL FY2025 10-K, p.8], [AAPL FY2025 10-K, p.17]
